# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.
# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

---

<!-- pack:tidy-repo -->
# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules

This is the Claudinite home repo's own local pack: the capture surface for lessons that are
**specific to working on the canon itself** and would not make sense mounted into a consuming
project. Portable lessons — anything true for repos beyond this one — belong in the shared canon
under `packs/`/`skills/` instead (proposed by PR, or lifted by the promote stage).

The growth lifecycle writes here automatically: the `growth-extract` and `conversation-extract`
daily tasks route the canon's own non-portable lessons into this pack (each at the local
promotion ladder's strongest mechanism — a check where the rule is deterministic, otherwise terse
prose below).

## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate

- **`canon-curation` lives in `.claudinite/local/packs/`, not `packs/`** (owner decision,
  2026-07-19). The canon home's curation duties are Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite —
  project-specific content on the home's own capture surface. Do not propose moving it back, and
  do not describe the move as open or provisional.
- **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling is ON — the fleet's default path** (same decision). The
  planner reads every member's local-pack daily descriptors by default; never reintroduce an
  "experimental / not enabled" framing or an opt-in seam for it.
- **Packs-tree segregation is barriers configuration only.** Any rule about what the `packs/`
  tree may reference is expressed by declaring/configuring the `barriers` pack (contributed
  edges, `siblings`/`scope` capabilities — extend barriers generically if a capability is
  missing). Never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation.
- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** (owner decision, 2026-07-23,
  #420). Status, phase tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation and remaining work live in that
  initiative's tracking issue (agent-preprocessing → #394); a phased plan lives in the sibling
  `MIGRATION.md`. Don't reintroduce a status / open-questions / remaining-work section there.
- **Multi-session work hands off through the tracking issue, never a prepared prompt** (owner
  correction, 2026-07-23). The owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so state not written
  into the issue is lost. Before ending a session on unfinished work, update the issue and let
  the session summary be a pointer to it — never compose a bespoke "pick up from here" prompt.

## Canon-specific gotchas

- **Baselining backfill skips the home — hand-declare fleet-seeded packs here.** The nightly
  baselining that lands a `seededByDefault` pack (and canon-delivered declaration changes) on
  every member is gated `!isHome`, so the canon home is the one repo it never reaches: a newly
  seeded pack does *not* arrive here automatically — the home's own `.claudinite-checks.json`
  must be updated by hand in the same change that flips the seed. The natural drift-guard (a
  future check, once the home is clean) is: the home declares every `seededByDefault` non-local
  pack.
- **The home doesn't declare `git-github`, so its skills never mount — never conclude "no such
  skill" from `.claude/skills/`.** `mount-skills.mjs` filters on the *literal* declaration
  (`isActive(p, { packs: declared })`), not the `requires` closure `check_the_world.mjs` resolves,
  and the baselining that would normalize that closure into `.claudinite-checks.json` is the one
  thing gated `!isHome` — so `merge-to-main` and `git-github-advanced` are simply absent here.
  Read `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree — the corpus *is* this repo,
  and an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. The seed-based
  drift-guard above would not catch this (`git-github` arrives by closure, never
  `seededByDefault`); a real one compares `resolveDeclaredPacks` against the literal declaration.
- **Never re-serialize a repo's JSON config to apply an edit — patch the text.** A round-trip
  rewrites what it wasn't asked to: Python's `json.dump` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True` (every
  non-ASCII character becomes a `\uXXXX` escape), and indent, key order and the trailing newline
  become the serializer's opinion. Nothing fails and tests stay green, so it rides onward. Edit
  JSON as anchored text; if you must round-trip, pin every lossy default and read the resulting
  diff before committing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `repo-text-sweeps`, where a
  `\uXXXX`-in-tracked-JSON check would carry it.)
- **Test git fixtures must commit with signing off.** `engine-tests/helpers.mjs`'s `makeRepo`
  overrides identity but not signing, so all 31 call sites route fixture commits through the
  signing service; when it degrades, each commit blocks on it and the suite leaks descriptors
  (~800 per full run against a 4096 cap) until `git commit` and `git push` fail process-wide.
  Commit with `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit --no-gpg-sign`: signing a tmpdir throwaway
  buys nothing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `writing-tests`.)
- **A canon session with a consumer repo also in its sources will reach for the *consumer's*
  merge skill — merge by the skill of the repo you are merging into.** Canon work is routinely
  dual-repo (the canon plus the fleet member being piloted), and both repos ship a merge skill
  under different names — the canon's `packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/` and, say, GCEC's
  local `merge-and-ci`. The consumer's skill wins the match on name/description and is followed
  to the letter, so the canon-only steps in *its* recipe are silently skipped — repeatedly, the
  **post-merge conversation capture** (`node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue
  <n>`, the "After the merge" section of `merge-to-main`). So: before merging in a dual-repo
  session, resolve the merge skill **by target repo**, not by which skill matched first — and
  treat capture as part of the merge, not as an optional epilogue.
- **Fail-soft SessionStart steps hide their own breakage fleet-wide — test the emitted
  output, not the exit code.** Every `engine/pack_loader/` SessionStart step
  (`inject-pack-prose.mjs`, `mount-skills.mjs`, `env-requirements.mjs`) wraps its body in
  `try { ... } catch {}` so a broken loader never blocks a session. That fail-soft is deliberate,
  but it means a runtime fault — a wrong dynamic-import target, a renamed module — exits 0 and
  simply emits nothing: no error, no signal. And because the engine is vendored verbatim into
  every member, one canon regression silently disables that step across the whole fleet at once.
  So a step like this must be guarded by a regression test that runs the real script against a
  real corpus and asserts the **positive** effect — prose IS emitted — never merely that
  `status === 0` (which fail-soft makes meaningless); see
  `engine-tests/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.test.mjs`.
- **The nightly self-refresh cannot repair the vendor-set computation — pin operational
  files against the REAL canon tree.** Baselining's converge re-runs
  `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs` from canon HEAD, so a bug *in that computation* is
  the one class of canon regression that is not self-healing: every refresh faithfully
  reproduces it, and recovery is an out-of-band vendor refresh applied to each member by
  hand. So when the vendor set excludes by *pattern*, an operational file that matches
  needs a by-path whitelist (`VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`) **and** a regression test asserting
  against the real canon tree, not only a synthetic fixture: a fixture keeps proving the
  whitelist mechanism works while the live path silently drops out from under it (see the
  paired tests in `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.test.mjs`).
- **You cannot force a due slot by running the scheduler workflow by hand.** Dueness is
  stateless — a slot is due iff its time falls in `(last successful run, now]` — so a
  `workflow_dispatch` run outside the slot's window succeeds, prints `- no tasks due`, and
  does nothing. It looks like a healthy run. To exercise a task Action-side, invoke its
  worker directly, or move the slot hour in `taskScheduler` and wait for the cron.
- **A code-search hit is evidence; a code-search miss is not — survey by reading each file.**
- **Derive the test file list from the tree — every hand-written glob here under-runs the suite.**
  There is no `package.json` and no test script, so each session invents its own incantation and
  silently verifies less than it thinks. Measured in this checkout: `node --test <dir>` does not
  recurse — it resolves the path as a module and dies with `Cannot find module`; bash `**` is not
  recursive without `globstar`, so `engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs` reaches
  **37 of 65** tracked test files. Four consecutive sessions (2026-07-26, #459/#452/#435/#468) each
  wrote a different command and reported 587, 690, 621 and 697 tests — three of them pushed after
  running a strict subset. Neither published list is authoritative either: `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)`
  array omits `vendoring/*.test.mjs`, and `engine/checks/README.md`'s "as CI runs it" one-liner
  names `engine/test/`, `skills/` and `mount/`, none of which exist. So enumerate from git and let
  the count speak: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. (The drift-guard, once the array is
  clean: assert every tracked `*.test.mjs` is matched by `ci.yml`'s globs.)
- **The home has no `.claudinite/shared/` mount — machinery paths must accept both roots.** A
  consumer runs the vendored engine under `.claudinite/shared/engine/…` with packs under
  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/packs/…`; the home *is* the corpus and runs the same code from the
  repo root. So a path, regex, or workflow command written to the consumer mount shape works
  fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — the last place anyone exercises it, so the break
  surfaces late. Write the two-root form up front: make the `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix
  optional in a pattern, and in a command probe for `.claudinite/shared/` first, falling back to
  the repo root.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. - authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- engineering-practices: General software-engineering practices — naming by scope, single-source-of-truth with drift guards, GENERATED-file discipline, earning each dependency, verifying real platform behavior. Use before writing or editing code.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location and test-location exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- prose-to-checks: Mine a repo's existing pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, or when the growth prose-to-checks sweep runs.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.

1	# Growth — extract lessons (per repo)
2	
3	The growth lifecycle's capture stage: review this repo's recent activity and fold any durable, reusable lesson into the repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/` — the normalized capture surface) — at the repo's own level, without straining to generalize it. It lands its edits through a PR that **auto-merges once the repo's checks pass** (no human review — the PR is armed for auto-merge, so daily capture never piles up as review requests); finding nothing to add on a given run is a perfectly good outcome.
4	
5	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the substantive commit shas and the PRs/issues touched in the window — that is the activity to mine; do not widen it.
6	
7	> This is the **unattended daily** capture. It writes only the repo's *own* local packs, so — **unlike** an owner-requested, in-session retrospective (which delivers a PR for a human to review) — it opens a PR and **arms auto-merge**: GitHub lands it once the repo's checks pass, with no review queue for daily lesson-capture to pile up in. The shared canon stays human-gated — lifting anything up into it is the central promote task's job (canon-side), and that PR waits for the owner.
8	
9	## Capture at the repo's own level
10	
11	Write each lesson at whatever level reads naturally for this repo — refer to its files, services, or mechanics wherever that's what makes the lesson clear, but don't force either extreme: don't contort a lesson to be hyper-specific, and don't polish it into a general, portable rule. Making a lesson portable is the central promote task's job, done canon-side later (it picks up whatever is merged here by its next run); here, just capture it usefully and let promotion lift whatever turns out to travel.
12	
13	## Conventions used in this doc
14	
15	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
16	- **GitHub access is MCP-native.** Reading issue/PR activity and updating the tracking issue go through the session's **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run has no shell GitHub access — the shell reaches only a git-over-HTTPS proxy scoped to one repo, with no REST credential — so never reach for `gh`/`curl` or a cross-repo clone.
17	- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) — everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename window), the repo's own packs; never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
18	
19	## How it finds lessons (scoped to the window in Context)
20	
21	1. **Read the window.** The window's **commits** (the shas named in Context — full bodies, diffs where a fix is non-obvious) and the **issue/PR activity** it names (the changed comments on those numbers). Where Context names PRs **merged in the window**, read those first and read them properly — the diff *and* the review discussion. 5	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the substantive commit shas and the PRs/issues touched in the window — that is the activity to mine; do not widen it.
6	
7	> This is the **unattended daily** capture. It writes only the repo's *own* local packs, so — **unlike** an owner-requested, in-session retrospective (which delivers a PR for a human to review) — it opens a PR and **arms auto-merge**: GitHub lands it once the repo's checks pass, with no review queue for daily lesson-capture to pile up in. The shared canon stays human-gated — lifting anything up into it is the central promote task's job (canon-side), and that PR waits for the owner.
8	
9	## Capture at the repo's own level
10	
11	Write each lesson at whatever level reads naturally for this repo — refer to its files, services, or mechanics wherever that's what makes the lesson clear, but don't force either extreme: don't contort a lesson to be hyper-specific, and don't polish it into a general, portable rule. Making a lesson portable is the central promote task's job, done canon-side later (it picks up whatever is merged here by its next run); here, just capture it usefully and let promotion lift whatever turns out to travel.
12	
13	## Conventions used in this doc
14	
15	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
16	- **GitHub access is MCP-native.** Reading issue/PR activity and updating the tracking issue go through the session's **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run has no shell GitHub access — the shell reaches only a git-over-HTTPS proxy scoped to one repo, with no REST credential — so never reach for `gh`/`curl` or a cross-repo clone.
17	- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) — everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename window), the repo's own packs; never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
18	
19	## How it finds lessons (scoped to the window in Context)
20	
21	1. **Read the window.** The window's **commits** (the shas named in Context — full bodies, diffs where a fix is non-obvious) and the **issue/PR activity** it names (the changed comments on those numbers). Where Context names PRs **merged in the window**, read those first and read them properly — the diff *and* the review discussion. A merged PR is usually the window's richest lesson source: it records what was tried, what a reviewer pushed back on, and why the landed shape won.
22	2. **Extract only durable, reusable lessons** — gotchas, engineering practices, test discipline, architecture rules, project mechanics — and **dedupe** each against what the repo already documents. When in doubt, leave it out.
23	3. **Route each lesson to the owning local pack, and prefer the strongest mechanism.** Pick the pack whose territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then run the **local promotion ladder**: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in that pack's `rules` (author the `.mjs`, list it on `pack.mjs`, add a red-first fixture — its failure message *is* the lesson), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack skill**, and only what neither can carry lands as terse **prose** in the pack's `RULES.md`. A gotcha tied to one call site still goes as a comment right at that site (the file-local rule — [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) owns the usage-site-vs-central call). Write more checks and less prose; keep each addition terse and in the repo's own voice.
24	
25	If an edit touches something a test reads (a doc constant, a code path), run the repo's offline test suite and keep it green before opening the PR.
26	
27	## Output: a PR that auto-merges after CI
28	
29	If it found at least one genuinely new lesson, it lands the edits **through a single auto-merging PR** — one commit for the whole run on a per-run-unique branch, not one per lesson. Open the PR (title `Claudinite growth: extract lessons`, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes) and **arm auto-merge**: GitHub squash-merges it once the repo's checks pass — no human review, so daily lesson-capture never floods review requests, while every change still gets a PR trail and a CI gate. Where the repo has no CI, GitHub lands it as soon as it's mergeable. This writes only the repo's *own* local packs (not the shared canon). A run that finds nothing and opens nothing is fine — and common. (A new check must ship green — see it fail on a violating fixture, pass on a clean one — so CI stays green and the PR can merge; a check that can't be made confident lands its lesson as prose instead, never a broken check.)
30	
31	## Tracking: log each run under the task's own issue
32	
33	The task's standing log is the issue titled exactly, in this repo:
34	
35	> **Claudinite tracker: Growth Extract**
36	
37	Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number** (a bare number can dangle, and it differs per repo). A run that finds no issue under the exact title just creates one (closed). **Never open, close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no meaning, only the log does. When a run adds a lesson, log it as a **dated comment** — not a sub-issue — so the issue accumulates a scrollable history, each entry naming **what was added and where**.
38	
39	## Run on a capable model
40	
41	Deciding whether a lesson is genuinely new and durable — and deduping it against what's already documented — is a **judgment call**, not mechanical extraction. A downgraded model adds noise or restates what's there, and **auto-merge means no human reviews the PR before it lands** — CI gates correctness, not whether a "lesson" earns its keep — so the capable-model requirement matters all the more. This task declares `agent_model: opus`; the executor dispatches its subagent there.
42	
43	## What this task must never do
44	
45	- **Never touch the shared canon** — this task writes only the repo's *own* local packs under `.claudinite/local/packs/`; everything else under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mount, and lifting a lesson up into the canon is the central promote task's job.
46	- **Never widen past the Context window** — the substantive commits and touched PRs/issues named there are the scope; do not re-decide it.
47	- **Don't add noise** — a duplicate or hallucinated "lesson" is worse than adding nothing, the more so when its PR auto-merges with no human review to catch it.

=== 0ba123e ===
0ba123e7d35aae3f3ef5da76f0d8386a85c39e99
The outside look: a sheepdog freshness sweep, and CI test roots that cannot silently under-run (#496)

* CI: sweep a closed set of test roots, and guard the set against drift

CI enumerated test paths one glob per directory depth
(`packs-tests/*/skills/*/*.test.mjs`, and eight more like it). `vendoring/`
matched none of them, so `apply-vendor-set.test.mjs` and
`compute-vendor-set.test.mjs` — 38 tests over the vendor computer and the
vendor writer, including the #328 anti-rewind guards — had never run in CI.
The suite was green over 719 of the repo's 757 tests and said nothing.

Depth is now out of the question: four roots, each swept with `**`.

  engine-tests/  packs-tests/  vendoring/  .claudinite/local/packs/

A test at any depth inside a root runs; the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/`
root, which has not existed since the local-pack path moved, is dropped.

A closed set only under-runs silently if nothing checks it, so
`engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs` parses the root list out of ci.yml —
the list is not duplicated, it is read from where CI actually uses it — and
asserts both directions: every tracked `*.test.mjs` falls under a root, and
every root still exists in the tree. Adding a root stays a deliberate CI
edit; adding a test does not.

Both assertions verified red first: dropping `vendoring/` names its two
files, and a fabricated root is reported as not in the tree.

Suite: 759 pass / 0 fail over all 67 tracked test files (up from 757 — the
two new guards). check_the_world: 0 blocking, 7 advisory, unchanged.

* sheepdog: sweep the fleet for members that have fallen behind canon

Per-project scheduling made every member maintain itself — its own vendored
`claudinite-scheduler.yml` fires hourly and its `baselining` task re-vendors
the mount. That is the right architecture, and it removed the last thing that
ever looked at a member from the OUTSIDE.

A member whose scheduler was never vendored, was deleted, or was auto-disabled
by GitHub after 60 quiet days is now invisible. It is still `covered` to the
census, because it still carries a declaration. It files no failure issue,
because nothing runs there to fail. Self-maintenance cannot detect its own
absence, and nothing else was looking.

Adds the sheepdog pack's second sweep — `check-fleet-freshness.mjs` and the
weekly agentless `fleet-freshness` task that runs it, the same shape the census
and `fleet-census` already have. Three reads per covered member (its
declaration, whether it carries the scheduler workflow, and canon's compare of
its stamped ref against canon's default branch), classified by ROOT CAUSE in
precedence order:

  no-stamp          declares packs, never vendored — no engine on disk
  no-scheduler      no cron, so nothing there will ever baseline it; every
                    other symptom is downstream of this one
  ref-not-on-trunk  the stamp is not an ancestor of canon's default branch, so
                    #328's anti-rewind guard REFUSES to write — wedged, not late
  behind            on trunk but stamped older than staleDays while canon moved

Precedence is the point, not an accident of the if-chain: a member with no
scheduler is also behind, and reporting "behind" sends the reader chasing a
symptom. Converges one `fleet-drift` issue per unhealthy member — a separate
label from the census's `fleet-adoption`, because the two close on unrelated
conditions — carrying the fix for the state it actually found.

The one assumption, stated in the code, the task doc and RULES.md rather than
buried: baselining reverts a stamp-only bump, so `claudinite.updated` advances
only when canon changed that member's vendor set. Age of the stamped REF is
therefore the honest liveness measure, and `behind` reads "has not picked canon
up in staleDays", not "canon moved". A member whose vendor set genuinely saw no
change in the window is the one false positive; `staleDays` (default 14) is the
knob and the issue body says so.

Quieter than the census by design: an open issue whose verdict is unchanged
gets no comment, so a fleet that heals slowly does not accumulate a wall of
identical weekly notes. The body carries a `<!-- fleet-freshness: state -->`
marker, so a changed root cause is noticed and reported with no cross-run state.

Same escalation rule the census keeps: a member that cannot be probed is
UNKNOWN, never behind — no issue opened, no open issue closed on its behalf,
and a non-zero exit the scheduler converges to `needs-human`.

`ensureLabel` and the labelled-issue read were identical in both sweeps and move
to `fleet-api.mjs`; the open/close POLICY stays in each sweep, where its
semantics are legible. `parseSheepdogConfig` gains `canonRepo` (default
`<owner>/Claudinite`) and `staleDays` (default 14) — both optional, so every
existing sheepdog config keeps working untouched, and one parser still reads the
pack entry.

No new PAT scope: Contents read and Issues read/write already cover it.

Verified: 778 pass / 0 fail (30 in packs-tests/sheepdog/, 19 new).
check_the_world 0 blocking / 7 advisory, unchanged. `computeVendorSet` over a
sheepdog declaration lands all six pack files; `discoverTasks` returns
`sheepdog/fleet-freshness | weekly | none | none` with no errors. Red-first:
inverting the precedence, commenting on an unchanged verdict, and closing an
UNKNOWN member as recovered each fail their test.

* DESIGN §6: record fleet-freshness in the task inventory

The design's task table is the inventory Phase 4 step 5 audits against, so a
task missing from it reads as a task that should not exist. fleet-freshness
was added after the design, by what the design caused — self-maintenance
removed the outside look at a member — and the row says exactly that rather
than pretending it was foreseen.

* sheepdog: each sweep lives in its task's folder; only the shared floor stays

A file whose only consumer is one task belongs in that task's folder. Both
sweeps sat at the pack root and neither was ever used from outside its task —
`check-fleet-coverage.mjs` only by `tasks/fleet-census/worker.mjs`,
`check-fleet-freshness.mjs` only by `tasks/fleet-freshness/worker.mjs`.

The reference-distance check never saw this: `../../check-fleet-coverage.mjs`
is distance 2, comfortably inside the threshold. Distance was the wrong
question. Sitting outside the task, a sweep advertises itself as a pack-level
surface — so the next author treats it as shared, and deleting the task would
strand it as orphaned code nobody dares remove.

  packs/sheepdog/check-fleet-coverage.mjs
    → packs/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-census/check-fleet-coverage.mjs
  packs/sheepdog/check-fleet-freshness.mjs
    → packs/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-freshness/check-fleet-freshness.mjs

Each worker's import collapses from `../../x.mjs` to `./x.mjs`, and each task
folder is now self-contained: declaration, spec, worker, and the code the
worker runs, travelling and deleting together.

`parseSheepdogConfig` blocked a clean move — it lived inside the census but
the freshness sweep imported it, so moving the census would have left one task
reaching sideways into another's folder. It is genuinely shared, so it is
lifted to the nearest common ancestor as `packs/sheepdog/fleet-config.mjs`,
beside `fleet-api.mjs`. The pack root now holds exactly what both tasks need
and nothing else.

Tests follow the source, mirroring the pack tree — and cost no CI edit, because
the preceding commit made CI sweep `packs-tests/` to any depth:

  packs-tests/sheepdog/{fleet-census,fleet-freshness}.test.mjs
    → packs-tests/sheepdog/tasks/<task>/task.test.mjs
  packs-tests/sheepdog/check-fleet-freshness.test.mjs
    → packs-tests/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-freshness/
  packs-tests/sheepdog/check-fleet-coverage.test.mjs
    → split into fleet-config.test.mjs + fleet-api.test.mjs

That last one tested no census code at all — it covered `parseSheepdogConfig`
and `isCovered`, both pack-root modules — so it followed what it actually
tests rather than the file it was named after.

The cross-sweep test now asserts the shape structurally: each sweep reaches UP
for `fleet-api.mjs` and `fleet-config.mjs`, never sideways into the other
task's folder, and carries no private copy of either.

The rule is recorded in the file-placement skill as its own section, since it
is a distinct axis from reference distance and the metric provably cannot
catch it.

Verified: 778 pass / 0 fail, unchanged. check_the_world 0 blocking / 7
advisory, unchanged. `computeVendorSet` lands all 13 sheepdog files at their
new paths; `discoverTasks` returns both tasks with zero errors; both workers
still run standalone from their task dirs and fail with the same escalation
message.

Wire the three signal-context keys nothing populated (#479)

engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs reads three keys off `ctx` that run.mjs's
construction never populated, so each fell through its `?? null` fallback on
every real run and the precondition arm it feeds was unreachable code:

- `ctx.manifestVersion` -> `release.manifestVersion`. store-release's
  manifest-ahead trigger was dead: the task could only fire on
  `commits.substantiveChange`, so a manifest bump that landed as a bot or
  housekeeping commit, or one whose release failed days ago, was never retried.
- `ctx.hasLocalPacks` -> `localPacks.present`. growth-dedup's "no local packs ->
  skip" arm was dead: `present` stayed null, never the explicit `false` the
  self-skip tests for, so a repo with zero local packs dispatched an opus agent
  on a 1800s budget to prune nothing.
- `ctx.retentionDays` -> `conversationLogs.retentionDays`. conversation-extract's
  age-based retention prune never fired. This one is a regression: the old form
  ran the prune weekly via `fullSweep`, retired on the stated grounds that this
  signal replaced it, so quiet repos' logs have been aging past retention with
  nothing to collect them.

The scheduler runs Action-side inside the checkout and run.mjs already holds
`root`, so all three are read from disk rather than over the API: no round-trip,
no rate budget, and the tree read is the tree the run would ship. The new
signals/local.mjs is the one place that touches the filesystem; the collectors
keep their `ctx.X ?? null` injection seam and still unit-test with no repo. The
manifest paths and leading-v tolerance are the retired run_daily gate's, and
retention is read through run.mjs's existing `packConfigFor` keyed by the
`retention_days` PARAMETER, so core names no pack. Local-pack roots now have one
definition shared by the presence probe and the changed-in-window probe.

No precondition logic, threshold, or context changed. Two preconditions now
reach arms they never could: growth-dedup skips (instead of dispatching) where a
repo has no local packs, and conversation-extract runs daily on a quiet repo
that has a logs branch and configured retention.

Each of the three had a unit test that hand-built a shape the collector could
not emit, so the suite was green while the plumbing was dead. Those unit seams
stay (the preconditions are pure functions worth testing directly) but now say
what they do not prove, and signal-context.test.mjs asserts reachability through
the real construction: a checkout on disk -> loadConfig -> buildSignalContext ->
collectSignals -> the actual precondition. It also carries the class guard —
every `ctx.<key>` the collectors read must be a key the real construction
produces, with the two legitimate exemptions named and justified — so the next
unwired ctx read fails a test instead of becoming a permanent null.

Also corrects the contract field name in five task docs that said `model:` where
the declaration field is `agent_model:` (growth-extract, growth-dedup,
conversation-extract, wiki-growth, repo-tidy).

tidy-repo: one task per dimension — issues, PRs, branches (#480)

The single `repo-tidy` pass did three unrelated jobs in one worker because the
reconcile needed all three dimensions' verdicts. Once each per-object verdict
moved into its own skill, that coupling was the only thing left holding them
together — and it dissolves the moment each dimension keeps its own tracker.

Three narrow tasks now, each triggered by the only thing that changes its
answers, scoped to exactly those objects, reconciling its own tracker:

- `tidy-issues` (daily, acts) — scope is the touched issues, widened to every
  open issue on a substantive default-branch move. That move is what can make an
  old issue implemented, so the full sweep is signal-triggered, not a calendar
  flag.
- `tidy-prs` (weekly, assess-only) — full every run: a PR verdict is a standing
  recommendation for a human, not a same-day alert.
- `tidy-branches` (weekly, assess-only) — full every run: the `branches` signal
  carries names only, so there is no windowed subset to narrow to, and branch
  cruft accumulates on a weekly clock.

Where a dimension needs a full run, it is the frequency DECLARATION — never a
`fullSweep` flag inside a daily task (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §3).

Each dimension gets its own tracker (`Claudinite tracker: Tidy Issues` / `Tidy
PRs` / `Tidy Branches`), so three independent tasks never race to rewrite one
body; the `tidy-issues` worker retires the combined legacy tracker in one
idempotent step.

Docs, the DESIGN §6 task table, the three skill descriptions, and the pack tests
follow. Both remaining preconditions are 3-5 lines, and a dimension with nothing
to do stays silent instead of riding along with the other two.

Closes #481

1	# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules
2	
3	This is the Claudinite home repo's own local pack: the capture surface for lessons that are
4	**specific to working on the canon itself** and would not make sense mounted into a consuming
5	project. Portable lessons — anything true for repos beyond this one — belong in the shared canon
6	under `packs/`/`skills/` instead (proposed by PR, or lifted by the promote stage).
7	
8	The growth lifecycle writes here automatically: the `growth-extract` and `conversation-extract`
9	daily tasks route the canon's own non-portable lessons into this pack (each at the local
10	promotion ladder's strongest mechanism — a check where the rule is deterministic, otherwise terse
11	prose below).
12	
13	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
14	
15	- **`canon-curation` lives in `.claudinite/local/packs/`, not `packs/`** (owner decision,
16	  2026-07-19). The canon home's curation duties are Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite —
17	  project-specific content on the home's own capture surface. Do not propose moving it back, and
18	  do not describe the move as open or provisional.
19	- **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling is ON — the fleet's default path** (same decision). The
20	  planner reads every member's local-pack daily descriptors by default; never reintroduce an
21	  "experimental / not enabled" framing or an opt-in seam for it.
22	- **Packs-tree segregation is barriers configuration only.** Any rule about what the `packs/`
23	  tree may reference is expressed by declaring/configuring the `barriers` pack (contributed
24	  edges, `siblings`/`scope` capabilities — extend barriers generically if a capability is
25	  missing). Never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation.
26	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** (owner decision, 2026-07-23,
27	  #420). Status, phase tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation and remaining work live in that
28	  initiative's tracking issue (agent-preprocessing → #394); a phased plan lives in the sibling
29	  `MIGRATION.md`. Don't reintroduce a status / open-questions / remaining-work section there.
30	- **Multi-session work hands off through the tracking issue, never a prepared prompt** (owner
31	  correction, 2026-07-23). The owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so state not written
32	  into the issue is lost. Before ending a session on unfinished work, update the issue and let
33	  the session summary be a pointer to it — never compose a bespoke "pick up from here" prompt.
34	
35	## Canon-specific gotchas
36	
37	- **Baselining backfill skips the home — hand-declare fleet-seeded packs here.** The nightly
38	  baselining that lands a `seededByDefault` pack (and canon-delivered declaration changes) on
39	  every member is gated `!isHome`, so the canon home is the one repo it never reaches: a newly
40	  seeded pack does *not* arrive here automatically — the home's own `.claudinite-checks.json`
41	  must be updated by hand in the same change that flips the seed. The natural drift-guard (a
42	  future check, once the home is clean) is: the home declares every `seededByDefault` non-local
43	  pack.
44	- **The home doesn't declare `git-github`, so its skills never mount — never conclude "no such
45	  skill" from `.claude/skills/`.** `mount-skills.mjs` filters on the *literal* declaration
46	  (`isActive(p, { packs: declared })`), not the `requires` closure `check_the_world.mjs` resolves,
47	  and the baselining that would normalize that closure into `.claudinite-checks.json` is the one
48	  thing gated `!isHome` — so `merge-to-main` and `git-github-advanced` are simply absent here.
49	  Read `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree — the corpus *is* this repo,
50	  and an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. The seed-based
51	  drift-guard above would not catch this (`git-github` arrives by closure, never
52	  `seededByDefault`); a real one compares `resolveDeclaredPacks` against the literal declaration.
53	- **Never re-serialize a repo's JSON config to apply an edit — patch the text.** A round-trip
54	  rewrites what it wasn't asked to: Python's `json.dump` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True` (every
55	  non-ASCII character becomes a `\uXXXX` escape), and indent, key order and the trailing newline
56	  become the serializer's opinion. Nothing fails and tests stay green, so it rides onward. Edit
57	  JSON as anchored text; if you must round-trip, pin every lossy default and read the resulting
58	  diff before committing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `repo-text-sweeps`, where a
59	  `\uXXXX`-in-tracked-JSON check would carry it.)
60	- **Test git fixtures must commit with signing off.** `engine-tests/helpers.mjs`'s `makeRepo`
61	  overrides identity but not signing, so all 31 call sites route fixture commits through the
62	  signing service; when it degrades, each commit blocks on it and the suite leaks descriptors
63	  (~800 per full run against a 4096 cap) until `git commit` and `git push` fail process-wide.
64	  Commit with `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit --no-gpg-sign`: signing a tmpdir throwaway
65	  buys nothing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `writing-tests`.)
66	- **A canon session with a consumer repo also in its sources will reach for the *consumer's*
67	  merge skill — merge by the skill of the repo you are merging into.** Canon work is routinely
68	  dual-repo (the canon plus the fleet member being piloted), and both repos ship a merge skill
69	  under different names — the canon's `packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/` and, say, GCEC's
70	  local `merge-and-ci`. The consumer's skill wins the match on name/description and is followed
71	  to the letter, so the canon-only steps in *its* recipe are silently skipped — repeatedly, the
72	  **post-merge conversation capture** (`node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue
73	  <n>`, the "After the merge" section of `merge-to-main`). So: before merging in a dual-repo
74	  session, resolve the merge skill **by target repo**, not by which skill matched first — and
75	  treat capture as part of the merge, not as an optional epilogue.
76	- **Fail-soft SessionStart steps hide their own breakage fleet-wide — test the emitted
77	  output, not the exit code.** Every `engine/pack_loader/` SessionStart step
78	  (`inject-pack-prose.mjs`, `mount-skills.mjs`, `env-requirements.mjs`) wraps its body in
79	  `try { ... } catch {}` so a broken loader never blocks a session. That fail-soft is deliberate,
80	  but it means a runtime fault — a wrong dynamic-import target, a renamed module — exits 0 and
81	  simply emits nothing: no error, no signal. And because the engine is vendored verbatim into
82	  every member, one canon regression silently disables that step across the whole fleet at once.
83	  So a step like this must be guarded by a regression test that runs the real script against a
84	  real corpus and asserts the **positive** effect — prose IS emitted — never merely that
85	  `status === 0` (which fail-soft makes meaningless); see
86	  `engine-tests/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.test.mjs`.
87	- **The nightly self-refresh cannot repair the vendor-set computation — pin operational
88	  files against the REAL canon tree.** Baselining's converge re-runs
89	  `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs` from canon HEAD, so a bug *in that computation* is
90	  the one class of canon regression that is not self-healing: every refresh faithfully
91	  reproduces it, and recovery is an out-of-band vendor refresh applied to each member by
92	  hand. So when the vendor set excludes by *pattern*, an operational file that matches
93	  needs a by-path whitelist (`VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`) **and** a regression test asserting
94	  against the real canon tree, not only a synthetic fixture: a fixture keeps proving the
95	  whitelist mechanism works while the live path silently drops out from under it (see the
96	  paired tests in `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.test.mjs`).
97	- **You cannot force a due slot by running the scheduler workflow by hand.** Dueness is
98	  stateless — a slot is due iff its time falls in `(last successful run, now]` — so a
99	  `workflow_dispatch` run outside the slot's window succeeds, prints `- no tasks due`, and
100	  does nothing. It looks like a healthy run. To exercise a task Action-side, invoke its
101	  worker directly, or move the slot hour in `taskScheduler` and wait for the cron.
102	- **A code-search hit is evidence; a code-search miss is not — survey by reading each file.**
103	- **Derive the test file list from the tree — every hand-written glob here under-runs the suite.**
104	  There is no `package.json` and no test script, so each session invents its own incantation and
105	  silently verifies less than it thinks. Measured in this checkout: `node --test <dir>` does not
106	  recurse — it resolves the path as a module and dies with `Cannot find module`; bash `**` is not
107	  recursive without `globstar`, so `engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs` reaches
108	  **37 of 65** tracked test files. Four consecutive sessions (2026-07-26, #459/#452/#435/#468) each
109	  wrote a different command and reported 587, 690, 621 and 697 tests — three of them pushed after
110	  running a strict subset. Neither published list is authoritative either: `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)`
111	  array omits `vendoring/*.test.mjs`, and `engine/checks/README.md`'s "as CI runs it" one-liner
112	  names `engine/test/`, `skills/` and `mount/`, none of which exist. So enumerate from git and let
113	  the count speak: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. (The drift-guard, once the array is
114	  clean: assert every tracked `*.test.mjs` is matched by `ci.yml`'s globs.)
115	- **The home has no `.claudinite/shared/` mount — machinery paths must accept both roots.** A
116	  consumer runs the vendored engine under `.claudinite/shared/engine/…` with packs under
117	  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/packs/…`; the home *is* the corpus and runs the same code from the
118	  repo root. So a path, regex, or workflow command written to the consumer mount shape works
119	  fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — the last place anyone exercises it, so the break
120	  surfaces late. Write the two-root form up front: make the `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix
121	  optional in a pattern, and in a command probe for `.claudinite/shared/` first, falling back to
122	  the repo root.

=== writing-tests SKILL ===
---
name: writing-tests
description: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
---

# Testing practices

Portable practices for writing tests you can actually trust — proving a test fails before relying on it, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, and how to gate a fuzzy quality metric. These are project-agnostic; a consuming repo's own test *mechanics* (runner, layout, which suites exist) stay in its own docs. (General software-engineering practices live in [the engineering-practices skill](../engineering-practices/SKILL.md); CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md).)

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. (A hostname-apex helper passed its tests but mis-stripped `tel-aviv.gov.il` → `gov.il`; the gap only surfaced when the function was run over the actual list of existing URLs.) Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (A UI-snapshot coverage gate parked behavioral leaves `9.1`–`9.3`/`3.4` and an unreachable `8.6` on cases that render none of them — issue #429.)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (The SPA-render fallback's CI test renders a `data:` URL whose script fills an empty root, not a real SPA — #310.)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

**2026-07-28** — dispatched by #500. Scope: commits `0ba123e`, `e22cde1`, `2f3e4e9`, `526c991`, `bca5ad4`; PRs #496/#465/#467/#493/#479/#480 (merged), #492/#497/#487 (touched); issues #498/#394/#391. No review discussion existed on any PR in the window, so every lesson came from commit bodies and diffs.

Two lessons, both into `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md` (Canon-specific gotchas) — proposed in **#502**, pending merge:

- **Enumerate tests by ROOT swept to any depth — a depth-enumerated glob list under-runs in silence.** From #496 / `0ba123e`: `vendoring/`'s 38 tests had never run in CI while the suite reported green over 719 of 757. Records the landed shape — four roots under `shopt -s globstar nullglob`, guarded by `engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs`, which parses the root list out of `ci.yml` itself rather than keeping a second copy that can drift.
- **A `ctx.X ?? null` injection seam hides dead wiring — pin the key set against the real construction.** From #479 / `526c991`: three signal keys were read by collectors and never populated by the construction, so each precondition arm was unreachable code while its unit test passed — the test hand-built a `ctx` shape the real construction could not emit. Names both guards the fix installed (an end-to-end test through the real construction, and a class guard over the key set).

Also **corrected** in the same file: the existing test-enumeration entry went stale in this same window — it still claimed `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)` array omits `vendoring/`, and still listed the drift-guard as future work. Both false now. Its live advice (`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`) and measured findings are preserved verbatim.

**Deduped out:** the one-consumer file-placement rule (#496, already in `packs/basics/skills/file-placement/SKILL.md`); the dedup-run scoping gotcha (#465, a file-local comment at its own call site); the `fullSweep`-vs-frequency-declaration rule (#480, per-project-scheduling DESIGN §3); the RULES.md tightening standard (#467, portable prose style rather than a canon-home gotcha).

Both landed as prose, not checks: in each case the deterministic half already ships as a test in the canon, and what remains is the generalized discipline.

Note: auto-merge could **not** be armed on #502 — GitHub rejects `enablePullRequestAutoMerge` with *"Protected branch rules not configured for this branch"*, since `main` carries no branch protection. The PR is left open for the owner to merge once CI is green (same path #489 took).

Added 2 lessons to `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md`, via **PR #437** (open — see the note at the bottom).

- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** — implementation status, phase/task tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation, and remaining work belong in that initiative's tracking issue, not the design doc. Recorded under *Standing owner decisions* (owner directive on #420, which stripped all of it out of `docs/agent-preprocessing/DESIGN.md` and pointed rollout status at #394).
- **The home has no `.claudinite/shared/` mount — machinery paths must accept both roots.** A consumer runs the vendored engine under `.claudinite/shared/engine/…` with packs under `.claudinite/(shared|local)/packs/…`; the canon home *is* the corpus and runs the same code from the repo root. So a path, regex, or workflow command written to the consumer mount shape works fleet-wide and fails on exactly one repo — this one, the last place anyone exercises it. It bit three surfaces in the single #421 cutover (`validate-dispatch`'s `DISPATCH_PATH_RE`, `executor.md`'s engine commands, `scheduler-workflow-shape`). Recorded under *Canon-specific gotchas* with the two-root shapes those adopted. Prose, not a check: the corpus legitimately names `.claudinite/shared/` throughout consumer-facing docs and stubs, so there is no false-positive-free signature.

Window scanned: the 38 substantive commits named in #428 plus PRs #424/#423/#410/#404/#401/#382/#380 and issues #394/#422/#418/#409/#408/#406/#381/#400/#379. The Phase 3 survey recorded TLDR as having no scheduled orchestrator when `chrome-extension-release.yml` carries `schedule: cron "0 3 * * *"`; the cutover would have gone red in the same commit under the blocking `gha/no-scheduled-fleet-executor`. Scope: this repo's own local packs only — no shared canon touched. `check_the_world --changed`: 0 blocking.
